claim: Motor contagions refer to implicit effects on one's actions induced by observed actions.
source: Motor contagions refer to implicit effects on one's actions induced by observed actions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided in the abstract that establishes the meaning of motor contagions.

claim: Motor contagions are believed to be induced simply by action observation.
source: Motor contagions are believed to be induced simply by action observation and cause an observer's action to become similar to the action observed.
evidence: This statement references established beliefs in the field about motor contagions, drawing on existing scientific understanding.

claim: Traditional motor contagions cause an observer's action to become similar to the action observed.
source: Motor contagions are believed to be induced simply by action observation and cause an observer's action to become similar to the action observed.
evidence: This describes the characteristic effect of traditional motor contagions based on established knowledge.

claim: A new motor contagion is induced only when observation is accompanied by prediction errors.
source: In contrast, here we report a new motor contagion that is induced only when the observation is accompanied by prediction errors - differences between actions one observes and those he/she predicts or expects.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Prediction errors are differences between actions one observes and those he/she predicts or expects.
source: prediction errors - differences between actions one observes and those he/she predicts or expects.
evidence: This is a definitional statement explaining what prediction errors are in the context of this study.

claim: The observation of the same action induces distinct motor contagions depending on whether prediction errors are present or not.
source: In two experiments, one on whole-body baseball pitching and another on simple arm reaching, we show that the observation of the same action induces distinct motor contagions, depending on whether prediction errors are present or not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both Experiment-1 and Experiment-2.

claim: In the absence of prediction errors, participants' actions changed to become similar to the observed action.
source: In the absence of prediction errors, as in previous reports, participants' actions changed to become similar to the observed action, while in the presence of prediction errors, their actions changed to diverge away from it, suggesting distinct effects of action observation and action prediction on human actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the nPE groups in both experiments.

claim: In the presence of prediction errors, participants' actions changed to diverge away from the observed action.
source: In the absence of prediction errors, as in previous reports, participants' actions changed to become similar to the observed action, while in the presence of prediction errors, their actions changed to diverge away from it, suggesting distinct effects of action observation and action prediction on human actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the PE groups in both experiments.

claim: Action observation and action prediction have distinct effects on human actions.
source: In the absence of prediction errors, as in previous reports, participants' actions changed to become similar to the observed action, while in the presence of prediction errors, their actions changed to diverge away from it, suggesting distinct effects of action observation and action prediction on human actions.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrasting results between nPE and PE groups.

claim: Motor behaviors are shaped by physical interactions with other individuals.
source: Our motor behaviors are shaped not just by physical interactions (Shergill et al., 2003; Ganesh et al., 2014; Takagi et al., 2017) but also by a variety of perceptual (Heyes, 2011; Chartrand and Bargh, 1999; Ikegami and Ganesh, 2014; Cook et al., 2012; Ganesh and Ikegami, 2016) interactions with other individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Motor behaviors are shaped by perceptual interactions with other individuals.
source: Our motor behaviors are shaped not just by physical interactions (Shergill et al., 2003; Ganesh et al., 2014; Takagi et al., 2017) but also by a variety of perceptual (Heyes, 2011; Chartrand and Bargh, 1999; Ikegami and Ganesh, 2014; Cook et al., 2012; Ganesh and Ikegami, 2016) interactions with other individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Motor contagions are the result of perceptual interaction.
source: Motor contagions are the result of such a perceptual interaction.
evidence: This statement draws on established understanding of motor contagions.

claim: Motor contagions refer to implicit changes in one's actions caused by the observation of the actions of others.
source: They refer to implicit changes in one's actions caused by the observation of the actions of others (Blakemore and Frith, 2005; Becchio et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Various motor contagions have been isolated in human behaviors over the past two decades.
source: Studies over the past two decades have isolated various motor contagions in human behaviors, from the so called automatic imitation (Brass et al., 2001; Heyes, 2011) and emulation (Edwards et al., 2003; Becchio et al., 2007; Gleissner et al., 2000), to outcome mimicry (Gray and Beilock, 2011) and motor mimicry (Chartrand and Bargh, 1999; Chartrand and Baaren, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Traditional motor contagions are induced simply by action observation.
source: These motor contagions are induced simply by action observation and have a signature characteristic - they cause certain features of one's action (such as kinematics [Brass et al., 2001; Heyes, 2011; Kilner et al., 2003], goal [Edwards et al., 2003; Becchio et al., 2007; Gleissner et al., 2000], or outcome [Gray and Beilock, 2011]) to become similar to that of the observed action.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Traditional motor contagions cause certain features of one's action to become similar to that of the observed action.
source: These motor contagions are induced simply by action observation and have a signature characteristic - they cause certain features of one's action (such as kinematics [Brass et al., 2001; Heyes, 2011; Kilner et al., 2003], goal [Edwards et al., 2003; Becchio et al., 2007; Gleissner et al., 2000], or outcome [Gray and Beilock, 2011]) to become similar to that of the observed action.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The new motor contagion is induced when observation is accompanied by prediction errors.
source: In contrast, here we report a new motor contagion that is induced not simply by action observation, but when the observation is accompanied by prediction errors - differences between actions one observes and those he/she predicts or expects.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The new motor contagion may not lead to similarities between observed actions and one's own actions.
source: Furthermore, this contagion may not lead to similarities between observed actions and one's own actions.
evidence: This is supported by data showing divergence in the PE groups.

claim: Distinct motor contagions are present in high dimensional whole body movement tasks such as baseball pitching.
source: We show that these contagions are present not only in high dimensional whole body movement tasks such as baseball pitching (Experiment-1) (Ikegami et al., 2017), but also simple day-to-day movement tasks such as arm reaching (Experiment-2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment-1.

claim: Distinct motor contagions are present in simple day-to-day movement tasks such as arm reaching.
source: We show that these contagions are present not only in high dimensional whole body movement tasks such as baseball pitching (Experiment-1) (Ikegami et al., 2017), but also simple day-to-day movement tasks such as arm reaching (Experiment-2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment-2.

claim: Thirty varsity baseball players participated in Experiment-1.
source: Thirty varsity baseball players participated in our Experiment-1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The sample size was determined by a power analysis.
source: The sample size was determined by a power analysis (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to determining sample size.

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups (n = 10 in each): No prediction error (nPE) group, Prediction error (PE) group, and Control (CON) group.
source: The participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups (n = 10 in each): No prediction error (nPE) group, Prediction error (PE) group, and Control (CON) group.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The participant's baseball experience was balanced across the three groups.
source: The participant's baseball experience was balanced across the three groups (F(2,27)=1.431, p=0.257, ηp2=0.096).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the participant characteristics.

claim: Participants in the nPE and PE groups performed five throwing sessions interspersed with four observation sessions.
source: The participants in the nPE and PE groups performed five throwing sessions (Figure 1A) that were interspersed with four observation sessions (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol, with reference to figures showing the setup.

claim: Participants in the CON group performed only the throwing sessions.
source: The participants in the CON group performed only the throwing sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the control group.

claim: CON group participants took a break between throwing sessions for a time period equivalent to the length of the observation sessions.
source: Instead of the observation sessions, they took a break in between the throwing sessions for a time period equivalent to the length of the observation sessions.
evidence: This describes the control condition protocol.

claim: Participants threw balls aimed for the center of a target while wearing occlusion goggles that turned opaque when the participant's arm crossed the infrared beam.
source: In the throwing task, the participants threw balls aimed for the center of a target while wearing 'occlusion' goggles, that turned opaque when the participant's arm crossed the infrared beam.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The occlusion goggles prevented participants from seeing where their throw hit the target.
source: This prevented them from seeing where their throw hit the target.
evidence: This describes the purpose and effect of the occlusion goggles.

claim: Each throwing session included ten throws.
source: Each throwing session included ten throws.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: In the observation session, participants watched a video of throws made by an unknown baseball pitcher.
source: In the observation session, the participants in the nPE and PE groups watched a video of throws made by an unknown baseball pitcher.
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: After each throw in the observation session, a numbered grid appeared on the target and participants were asked to report the grid number corresponding to where the ball hit the target.
source: After each throw, a numbered grid (see Figure 1B) appeared on the target (in the video) once the ball hit the target, and the participants were asked to report the grid number corresponding to where they saw the ball hit the target.
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: The purpose of the reporting task was to ensure that participants maintained their attention on the target in the video.
source: The purpose of this reporting task was to ensure that the participants maintained their attention on the target in the video.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the reporting task.

claim: Half the participants in each group were shown throws that predominantly hit the upper-right corner of the target.
source: To cancel out any spatial bias with respect to the observed actions, half the participants in each group (called upper-right observing participants) were shown throws that predominantly hit the upper-right corner of the target (most frequent at #3, see yellow gradient Figure 2B and Materials and methods for observed throw distribution).
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for spatial bias.

claim: The other five participants in each group were shown a video of throws predominantly hitting the lower-left corner of the target.
source: The other five participants (called lower-left observing participants) were shown a video of throws predominantly hitting the lower-left corner of the target (most frequent at #7, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for spatial bias.

claim: Each observation session included 20 observed throws.
source: Each observation session included 20 observed throws.
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: Different instructions were provided to the nPE and PE groups to manipulate the prediction errors induced in them.
source: Different instructions were provided to the nPE and PE groups to manipulate the prediction errors induced in them.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: Participants in the nPE group were told that the pitcher in the video was aiming for different grid numbers on the target across trials and only successful trials were displayed.
source: The participants in the nPE group were told that 'the pitcher in the video is aiming for different grid numbers on the target across trials. These numbers were provided by the experimenter and we display only those trials in which he was successful in hitting the number he aimed for'.
evidence: This describes the instruction given to the nPE group.

claim: Participants in the PE group were instructed that the pitcher in the video was aiming for the center of the target.
source: On the other hand, participants in the PE group were instructed that 'the pitcher in the video is aiming for the center of the target'.
evidence: This describes the instruction given to the PE group.

claim: The two different instructions were designed to lead to greater prediction errors in the PE group compared with the nPE group.
source: The two different instructions were designed to lead to greater prediction errors in the PE group compared with the nPE group.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the different instructions.

claim: The instruction to the nPE group was expected to attenuate any prediction error.
source: The instruction to the nPE group prevents the participants from having any prior expectation of the outcome of an observed throw, and was thus expected to attenuate any prediction error.
evidence: This explains the expected effect of the nPE instruction.

claim: The instruction to the PE group was expected to induce a difference between the throw outcome expected by the participants and the actual outcome observed by them.
source: In contrast, the instruction to the PE group makes the participants expect the observed throws to hit near the target center. Similar to previous studies (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2014; Ondobaka et al., 2015), this instruction was thus expected to induce a difference between the throw outcome expected by the participants and the actual outcome observed by them.
evidence: This explains the expected effect of the PE instruction, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The accuracy of the report in the observation session was comparable between the nPE and PE groups.
source: First, in the observation session, the accuracy (% correct) of the report was comparable between the two groups (nPE: 96.25 ± 1.48 (mean ± s.d.) %, PE: 95.63 ± 3.32 %; two sample t-test, t(18)=0.516, p=0.612).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the observation task performance.

claim: The comparable accuracy ensures that the level of attention to the video was similar between the two groups.
source: This ensures that the level of attention to the video was similar between the two groups.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparable accuracy data.

claim: The performance in the throwing session dramatically differed between the nPE and PE groups.
source: The performance in the throwing session, however, dramatically differed between the two groups.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the detailed statistical analyses that follow.

claim: The throws by the nPE group progressively drifted towards where the pitcher in the video predominantly threw the ball.
source: The throws by the nPE group progressively drifted towards where the pitcher in the video predominantly threw the ball (blue data in Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claim: The pattern in the nPE group is similar to the motor contagion reported previously as outcome mimicry.
source: This pattern is similar to the motor contagion reported previously as outcome mimicry (Gray and Beilock, 2011).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The throws by the PE group progressively drifted away from where the pitcher in the video predominantly threw the ball.
source: In contrast, the throws by the PE group progressively drifted away from where the pitcher in the video predominantly threw the ball (red data in Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claim: The hit locations along the parallel diagonal showed a significant interaction between the sessions and groups.
source: The hit locations along the parallel diagonal (Figure 3) showed a significant interaction between the sessions and groups (F(8,108)=5.124, p=2 × 10−5, ηp2=0.275).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Across the sessions, the throws in the nPE group significantly drifted towards the direction of observed pitcher's throws.
source: Across the sessions, the throws in the nPE group (blue data in Figures 2B and 3) significantly drifted towards the direction of observed pitcher's throws (F(4,36)=2.910, p=0.035, ηp2=0.244; first vs fifth sessions by Tukey's test: p=0.034)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The throws in the PE group significantly drifted away from the observed pitcher's throws.
source: while the throws in the PE group (red data in Figures 2B and 3) significantly drifted away from the observed pitcher's throws (F(4,36)=5.170, p=2 × 10−3, ηp2=0.365; first vs fifth sessions by Tukey's test: p=5 × 10−3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The throws in the CON group did not show a drift along the parallel diagonal.
source: The throws in the CON group (black data in Figures 2A and 3) did not show such a drift (F(4,36)=0.297, p=0.878, ηp2=0.032) along the parallel diagonal.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: The hit locations along the orthogonal diagonal in all the nPE, PE, and CON groups showed no significant differences across the throwing sessions.
source: On the other hand, the hit locations along the orthogonal diagonal in all the nPE, PE, and CON groups showed no significant differences across the throwing sessions (F(4,108)=1.762, p=0.142, ηp2=0.061) and between the groups (F(2,27)=1.150, p=0.332, ηp2=0.079).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The lack of drift along the orthogonal diagonal confirms that the drifts observed in the nPE and PE groups are not the result of possible cognitive fatigue induced by the extra observation task.
source: This result confirms that the drifts observed in the nPE and PE groups are not the result of possible cognitive fatigue induced by the extra observation task they performed (compared with the CON group), or cognitive biases induced by the validity of the instructions given to them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of drift along the orthogonal diagonal.

claim: The focused drifts along the parallel diagonal suggest that the drifts were induced by the bias in the observed pitcher's throws (in the nPE group) and the prediction errors (in the PE group).
source: The focused drifts along the parallel diagonal suggest that the drifts were induced by the bias in the observed pitcher's throws (in the nPE group) and the prediction errors (in the PE group), both of which were present specifically along the parallel diagonal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results.

claim: The effects of observed actions on the participants' actions emerged as an increase in spatial bias but not in spatial variability in their action outcome.
source: In addition, the effects of observed actions on the participants' actions emerged as an increase in spatial bias but not in spatial variability in their action outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of within-participant variability.

claim: For the orthogonal diagonal, the within-participant variability in hit locations showed no significant differences across the sessions in all three groups.
source: For the orthogonal diagonal, the within-participant variability in their hit locations, measured by variance in each throwing session (see Materials and methods), showed no significant differences across the sessions in all the three groups (Friedman' test, nPE: χ2(4)=7.44, p=0.114; PE: χ2(4)=0.32, p=0.989; CON: χ2(4)=3.2, p=0.525).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: For the parallel diagonal, the PE group showed a significant change in variance.
source: For the parallel diagonal, although the PE groups showed a significant change in variance (nPE: χ2(4)=3.28, p=0.512; PE: χ2(4)=10.48, p=0.033; CON: χ2(4)=3.2, p=0.525), we did not observe any clear trend in the median values of the within-participant variability across the sessions
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No clear trend was observed in the median values of the within-participant variability across the sessions for the parallel diagonal in the PE group.
source: we did not observe any clear trend in the median values of the within-participant variability across the sessions (first session: 7.772; second: 5.360; third: 7.092; fourth: 7.008; fifth: 7.767 × 104 mm2, respectively).
evidence: This is based on examination of the median values across sessions.

claim: A post hoc analysis found no significant difference between any pair of sessions for within-participant variability along the parallel diagonal.
source: And, a post hoc analysis found no significant difference between any pair of sessions (Wilcoxon signed rank test, Zs <1.886, ps >0.059, which was considerably above the Bonferroni corrected significance level of p=0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The observation of a same action can lead to distinct motor contagions depending on whether the observation takes place in the presence or absence of prediction errors.
source: Together, these results clearly show that the observation of a same action can lead to distinct motor contagions depending on whether the observation takes place in the presence or absence of prediction errors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the Experiment-1 results.

claim: Experiment-2 was conducted to check whether the prediction error induced contagion is specific to sports experts.
source: Next, to check whether this prediction error induced contagion is specific to sports experts, and to verify whether it can also be observed in simple everyday movement tasks, we conducted a second follow-up experiment in which we used a similar experimental design to before but tested average adult participants in an arm reaching task (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This explains the rationale for Experiment-2.

claim: Experiment-2 was conducted to verify whether the prediction error induced contagion can be observed in simple everyday movement tasks.
source: Next, to check whether this prediction error induced contagion is specific to sports experts, and to verify whether it can also be observed in simple everyday movement tasks, we conducted a second follow-up experiment in which we used a similar experimental design to before but tested average adult participants in an arm reaching task (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This explains the rationale for Experiment-2.

claim: Thirty right-handed averaged male participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups (n = 10 in each): nPE, PE, and CON groups in Experiment-2.
source: Thirty right-handed averaged male participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups (n = 10 in each): nPE, PE, and CON groups.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment-2.

claim: Participants in the nPE and PE groups performed five reaching sessions and four observation sessions in Experiment-2.
source: The participants in the nPE and PE groups performed five reaching sessions and four observation sessions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol of Experiment-2.

claim: Participants in the CON group performed only the reaching sessions in Experiment-2.
source: The participants in the CON group performed only the reaching sessions.
evidence: This describes the control condition in Experiment-2.

claim: Participants wore occlusion goggles which became opaque as soon as their arm movements started in the reaching task.
source: They again wore occlusion goggles which, similar to the throwing experiment, became opaque as soon as their arm movements started, preventing them from observing where their finger touched the screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each reaching session included ten reaches.
source: Each reaching session included ten reaches.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: In the observation session of Experiment-2, participants watched a video of an unknown individual reaching towards the same touch screen.
source: In the observation session, the participants in the nPE and PE groups watched a video of an unknown individual (henceforth, the actor) reaching towards the same touch screen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: After each reach in the observation session, participants were asked to report if the actor had touched the 'right', 'left', or 'outside' area.
source: After each reach, the participants were asked to report if the actor had touched the 'right' (area between the center and right lines), 'left' (area between the center and left lines), or 'outside' (of the right and left lines).
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: Half the participants in each group watched a video showing the actor predominantly touching the right area.
source: Half the participants in each group watched a video showing the actor predominantly touching the right area (called right observing participants), and the other half watched a video showing the actor predominantly touching the left area (called left observing participants), respectively (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each observation session in Experiment-2 included 20 observed reaches.
source: Each observation session included 20 observed reaches.
evidence: This describes the observation task protocol.

claim: Different instructions were provided to the nPE and PE groups in Experiment-2 to manipulate the prediction errors.
source: To manipulate the prediction errors, we again provided different instructions to the nPE and PE groups.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: For the nPE group in Experiment-2, the right and left observing participants were told that the actor was aiming for the right area and left area, respectively.
source: For the nPE group, the right and left observing participants were told that 'the actor in the video is aiming for the right area' and 'the actor in the video is aiming for the left area', respectively.
evidence: This describes the instruction given to the nPE group.

claim: The instruction to the nPE group in Experiment-2 was expected to minimize the difference between the actor's touch location expected by the participants and the actual location observed by them.
source: This instruction was expected to minimize the difference between the actor's touch location expected by the participants, and the actual location observed by them, thus leading to suppression in prediction errors.
evidence: This explains the expected effect of the nPE instruction.

claim: Participants in the PE group in Experiment-2 were instructed that the actor was aiming for the center line.
source: On the other hand, participants in the PE group were instructed that 'the actor in the video is aiming for the center line'.
evidence: This describes the instruction given to the PE group.

claim: The instruction to the PE group in Experiment-2 was expected to induce substantial prediction errors.
source: This instruction was expected to induce substantial prediction errors as in Experiment-1.
evidence: This explains the expected effect of the PE instruction.

claim: The accuracy of the report in the observation session of Experiment-2 was comparable between the nPE and PE groups.
source: First, in the observation session, we confirmed that the accuracy (% correct) of the report was comparable between the two groups (nPE: 93.20 ± 3.94 (mean ± s.d.) %, PE: 93.00 ± 5.10 %; two sample t-test, t(18)=0.098, p=0.923).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment-2, similar results to Experiment-1 were observed in the reaching session.
source: Next, in the reaching session, we observed similar results to Experiment-1
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing results across experiments.

claim: The touch locations by the participants in Experiment-2 showed significant interaction between the sessions and groups.
source: the touch locations by the participants (Figure 4B) showed significant interaction between the sessions and groups (F(8,108)=2.568, p=0.013, ηp2=0.160).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Across the sessions in Experiment-2, the touch locations by the nPE group drifted towards the direction of observed actor's touch locations.
source: Across the sessions, the touch locations by the nPE group (blue data in Figure 4B) drifted towards the direction of observed actor's touch locations (F(4,36)=2.307, p=0.077, ηp2=0.204), although it marginally missed statistical significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, though statistical significance was marginal.

claim: The touch locations by the PE group in Experiment-2 significantly drifted away from the direction of the observed actor's touch locations.
source: More importantly for this study, the touch locations by the PE group (red data in Figure 4B) significantly drifted away from the direction of the observed actor's touch locations (F(4,36)=2.683, p=0.047, ηp2=0.230).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The touch locations in the CON group in Experiment-2 did not show any substantial change.
source: The touch locations in the CON group (black data in Figure 4B) did not show any substantial change (F(4,36)=0.639, p=0.638, ηp2=0.066).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The within-participant variability in touch locations in Experiment-2 showed no significant differences across the reaching sessions.
source: In addition, the within-participant variability in their touch locations showed no significant differences across the reaching sessions (nPE: χ2(4)=5.04, p=0.283; PE χ2(4)=4.80, p=0.308; CON: χ2(4)=9.44, p=0.051).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Experiment-2 successfully reproduced the Experiment-1 results.
source: Thus, Experiment-2 successfully reproduced the Experiment-1 results, which suggests that the two distinct motor contagions can affect even basic everyday movements like arm reaching.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing the two experiments.

claim: The two distinct motor contagions can affect even basic everyday movements like arm reaching.
source: Thus, Experiment-2 successfully reproduced the Experiment-1 results, which suggests that the two distinct motor contagions can affect even basic everyday movements like arm reaching.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful replication in Experiment-2.

claim: The clear motor performance changes in the PE groups observed in the two experiments validate the presence of a new motor contagion which is induced by prediction errors during action observation.
source: Crucially, the clear motor performance changes in the PE groups observed in the two experiments validate the presence of a new motor contagion which is induced by prediction errors during action observation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from both experiments.

claim: Previous motor contagion studies have extensively examined how observation of the actions of others affects action production.
source: Previous motor contagion studies have extensively examined how observation of the actions of others affects action production (Heyes, 2011; Chartrand and Bargh, 1999; Becchio et al., 2007; Brass et al., 2001; Edwards et al., 2003; Gray and Beilock, 2011; Kilner et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous action prediction studies have examined how action production affects prediction of observed actions.
source: On the other hand, while previous action prediction studies have examined how action production (Mulligan et al., 2016; Hamilton et al., 2004), or the ability to produce an action (Knoblich and Flach, 2001; Urgesi et al., 2012; Kanakogi and Itakura, 2011) affects prediction of observed actions, the converse, the effect of action prediction on one's actions, has rarely been examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effect of action prediction on one's actions has rarely been examined.
source: the converse, the effect of action prediction on one's actions, has rarely been examined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: A previous study reported that an improvement in the ability to predict observed actions affects the observer's ability to produce the same action.
source: One exception is our previous study (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2014), which reported that an improvement in the ability to predict observed actions affects the observer's ability to produce the same action.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The observations from the previous study are likely to be a prediction error induced motor contagion.
source: The observations from this previous study are likely to be a prediction error induced motor contagion, but as the direction of the observed actions and the corresponding prediction errors were not controlled in the study, it was difficult to conclude this cause.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of previous findings.

claim: The effects of action prediction and action observation on action production have never been compared.
source: Overall, the effects of action prediction and action observation on action production have never been compared.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: This study compares the effects of action prediction and action observation on action production for the first time.
source: This study compares the two effects for the first time by modulating the prediction errors perceived by participants, when they observe throws or reaches by another individual.
evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the current study.

claim: Previously reported motor contagions are believed to be caused by the presence of long-term sensorimotor associations.
source: The previously reported motor contagions are believed to be caused by the presence of 'long-term' sensorimotor associations (Heyes, 2011; Cook et al., 2014), in which an observed action automatically activates an individual's sensorimotor representations of the same action, making his/her actions similar to the observed actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Further studies are required to understand the mechanisms underlying the prediction error induced motor contagion.
source: While further studies are required to understand the mechanisms underlying the prediction error induced motor contagion, it is still interesting to note the parallel between this motor contagion and behavioral characteristic of motor learning.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and suggests future research directions.

claim: When learning a new motor task, individuals are believed to utilize prediction errors from self-generated actions to change their sensorimotor associations and correct their actions.
source: When learning a new motor task, individuals are believed to utilize prediction errors from self-generated actions to change their sensorimotor associations, and correct their actions (Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on motor learning.

claim: The motor contagion in the PE group seems to cause participants to make similar action corrections to compensate for their prediction errors, even though the prediction errors are from actions made by another individual.
source: The motor contagion in the PE group seems to cause participants to make similar action corrections to compensate for their prediction errors, strangely even though the prediction errors are from actions made by another (observed) individual, rather than from self-generated actions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Previously reported motor contagions may be explained as a facilitation/interference in action production by the sensorimotor associations activated by observed actions.
source: Therefore, while the previously reported motor contagions may be explained as a facilitation/interference in action production by the sensorimotor associations (Heyes, 2011; Cook et al., 2014) activated by observed actions, the new contagion we present here is probably a result of erroneous changes in the sensorimotor associations, caused by the observed prediction errors (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The new contagion is probably a result of erroneous changes in the sensorimotor associations, caused by the observed prediction errors.
source: Therefore, while the previously reported motor contagions may be explained as a facilitation/interference in action production by the sensorimotor associations (Heyes, 2011; Cook et al., 2014) activated by observed actions, the new contagion we present here is probably a result of erroneous changes in the sensorimotor associations, caused by the observed prediction errors (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The prediction error induced contagions seem similar to the phenomena of observational motor learning.
source: The prediction error induced contagions presented here seem similar to the phenomena of observational motor learning, in which the observation of an action is reported to aid subsequent motor learning (Adams, 1986; Schmidt and Lee, 2005; Mattar and Gribble, 2005; Buckingham et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has been suggested that observational motor learning is possible because of an observation induced adaptation of the inverse model that determines motor commands for a given task.
source: It has been suggested that observational motor learning is possible because of an observation induced adaptation of the inverse model (or controller) that determines motor commands for a given task (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In a recent study, the behavioral changes resulting from prediction error induced contagions can be explained only by an influence in an individual's forward model.
source: On the other hand, in a recent study (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2017), we showed that the behavioral changes resulting from prediction error induced contagions can be explained only by an influence in an individual's forward model, that uses the motor commands to estimate one's movement outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The difference in effects between observational motor learning and prediction error induced contagions could result from the lack of an explicitly required learning in the contagion studies.
source: This difference in effects could result from two factors. First, unlike observational motor learning (Maslovat et al., 2010; Ong et al., 2012), our previous (Ikegami and Ganesh, 2014; Ikegami and Ganesh, 2017) and present studies did not require the participants to learn a new motor task, and in fact included participants who were arguably over-trained in the task. This strongly suggests that the contagion effects in these studies are implicit (not willed by the participants).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation comparing different phenomena.

claim: The contagion effects in these studies are implicit (not willed by the participants).
source: This strongly suggests that the contagion effects in these studies are implicit (not willed by the participants).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design.

claim: The difference in effects could result from the systematic manipulation of participants' belief regarding the observed actions to control the direction of prediction errors.
source: And second, unlike the observational motor learning studies, this study systematically manipulates the participants' belief regarding the observed actions to control the direction of prediction errors.
evidence: This describes a key methodological difference.

claim: The lack of an explicitly required learning and the effect of belief are probably key to whether and to what extent observed actions affect the inverse or forward modeling process, or both.
source: The lack of an explicitly required learning and the effect of belief are probably key to whether and to what extent, observed actions affect the inverse, or forward modeling process, or both.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between phenomena.

claim: Further studies are required to address whether observed actions affect the inverse or forward modeling process, or both.
source: However, further studies are required to address this question concretely.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and suggests future research.

claim: Further studies are needed to examine whether the prediction error induced motor contagions play a functional role in motor actions.
source: Finally, further studies are also needed to examine whether the prediction error induced motor contagions play a functional role in our motor actions.
evidence: This suggests a direction for future research.

claim: If the contagions contribute to motor skill acquisition or motor adaptation to a new environment, the phenomenon may need to be re-defined as a new learning process rather than a new motor contagion.
source: If the contagions are proved to contribute to motor skill acquisition or motor adaptation to a new environment, we may need to re-define the phenomenon as a new learning process rather than a new motor contagion.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of future findings.

claim: Understanding the interactions between the distinct effects of action observation and action prediction is arguably critical for the complete understanding of human skill learning.
source: In conclusion, our results clearly show that action observation and action prediction can induce distinct effects on an observer's actions. Understanding the interactions between these distinct effects is arguably critical for the complete understanding of human skill learning.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Understanding the interactions between action observation and action prediction effects can enable a better understanding of the link between the mechanisms of motor contagions and motor learning.
source: For example, it can enable a better understanding of the link between the mechanisms of motor contagions and motor learning, and help develop better procedures to improve motor performances in sports and rehabilitation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.
